extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical political economy; economists and general readers interested in wages, profit, and the division of labour
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and apply the classical determinants and comparative principles that govern wages and profits across different employments — e.g., agreeableness, cost of learning, constancy of employment, trust, probability of success, and risk. The page sets out how these factors operate and gives illustrative examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion of market interest to ordinary clear profit
rubrics_metrics.description: The proportion which the usual market rate of interest ought to bear to the ordinary rate of clear profit necessarily varies as profit rises or falls. 'Double interest' is reckoned a good, moderate, reasonable profit in Great Britain; in countries where ordinary clear profit is 8–10%, one half may reasonably go to interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interest compensates the lender for insuring the stock and the trouble of employing it; e.g., 4–5% interest may be sufficient in many trades when ordinary profit is higher. The proportion may differ where ordinary profits are much lower or higher.

rubrics_metrics.name: High profits raise commodity prices via geometric accumulation
rubrics_metrics.description: High profits operate like compound interest through the successive stages of manufacture, raising the price of commodities more strongly than equivalent increases in wages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: If employers at each stage require an additional 5% profit on the advanced price (materials + wages), the price increase compounds at each stage (geometrical progression), whereas wage increases add arithmetically across stages. The linen-manufacture example illustrates this contrast between profit (compound) and wage (simple) effects on final price.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency toward equality of advantages across employments (mobility/equalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the same neighbourhood, advantages and disadvantages of different employments must be either perfectly equal or continually tending to equality because people will crowd into more advantageous employments and desert less advantageous ones where there is perfect liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This equalization presumes free choice of occupation and mobility; deviations arise from local circumstances or policy constraints that prevent perfect liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreeableness or disagreeableness of the employment
rubrics_metrics.description: The wages of labour vary with the agreeableness or disagreeableness (cleanliness or dirtiness, honourableness or dishonourableness) of the employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: journeyman tailor (easier) earns less than journeyman weaver; journeyman blacksmith vs collier; butchers and public executioners are better paid because of disagreeableness or disgrace. Agreeableness/disagreeableness also affects profits of stock in similar fashion where relevant (e.g., tavern-keeper's trade yielding large profit despite disagreeableness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Easiness/cheapness or difficulty/expense of learning the trade (skill and training costs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wages vary with the easiness and cheapness, or the difficulty and expense, of learning the business — expensive or lengthy education/ apprenticeship must be remunerated by higher wages to compensate the cost and time of acquiring skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apprenticeship rules, parental maintenance during training, and fees to masters are factors. Skilled trades' higher wages should just compensate the expense of education; more tedious education (liberal professions, arts) should command still greater pecuniary recompense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constancy versus inconstancy of employment
rubrics_metrics.description: Wages in different occupations vary with the constancy or inconstancy of employment: trades with intermittent work command higher day-wages to compensate for periods of unemployment and anxiety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: masons and bricklayers earn substantially more than steady manufacturers due to weather/dependent demand; journeymen tailors in London suffer intermittent employment and earn more to compensate. When inconstancy combines with disagreeableness, wages can be especially high (colliers, coal-heavers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Amount of trust reposed in workers
rubrics_metrics.description: Wages vary according to the small or great trust which must be reposed in the workmen; occupations entrusted with valuables, health, fortune, or reputation command higher wages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: goldsmiths and jewellers, physicians, and lawyers earn more because important trust requires them to have social rank and recompense; this combines with education costs to raise their pay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability or improbability of success in an occupation (lottery effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wages in occupations vary according to the probability or improbability of success: professions where few succeed must pay successful practitioners enough to compensate for many unsuccessful aspirants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: law — many students never make a living; the one who succeeds should gain the retribution of many unsuccessful ones, partially explaining high fees. The 'lottery' analogy and the human overvaluation of chance are used to explain entry into risky or low-return professions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk and uncertainty of returns raising ordinary profit (but not proportionally)
rubrics_metrics.description: In employments of stock, the ordinary rate of profit varies with the certainty or uncertainty of returns: profit tends to rise with risk, but not necessarily in proportion to it; hazardous trades experience more bankruptcies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: foreign trade branches differ in ordinary profit according to risk (e.g., trade to North America vs Jamaica); smuggling can be most profitable when successful but leads to frequent bankruptcy. Competition and over-entrance into hazardous trades can reduce average profit below what would fully compensate risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only agreeableness and risk of trade materially affect profits of stock
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the five circumstances that vary wages, only two — the agreeableness/disagreeableness of the business and the risk or security with which it is attended — significantly affect the ordinary profits of stock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other wage determinants (learning cost, constancy, trust, probability of success) influence labour earnings more than ordinary profit rates of stock; thus profits across trades tend to be more equal than wages across occupations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unwholesomeness classified as disagreeableness raising wages
rubrics_metrics.description: Unwholesome employments (those injurious to health) are a species of disagreeableness and command remarkably high wages to compensate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unwholesomeness is treated alongside dirtiness and danger as reasons why certain labourers earn premiums; it does not raise profits of stock except insofar as it affects agreeableness of the business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constancy of employment does not affect ordinary profits of stock
rubrics_metrics.description: The constancy or inconstancy of employment cannot affect the ordinary profits of stock in any particular trade; whether stock is constantly employed depends on the trader, not the trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This contrasts with labour wages, where constancy is a key determinant; thus profit rates across trades remain fairly uniform irrespective of employment constancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparent profits may be wages disguised as profit (price structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: In some trades the apparent profit (large percentage on goods sold) is actually the reasonable wages of labour disguised as profit — e.g., apothecaries charging high markups on drugs may be remunerating skill, trust, and learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: apothecary who sells a small annual quantity of drugs at very high markups may nonetheless be receiving compensation for skill/trust rather than pure profit; differentiate what should be considered wages from true profit when comparing trades.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market size, capital, and narrowness influence apparent profit rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Smaller trades or narrow markets may show very high percentage profits on small capital, while large-scale merchants earn lower percentage returns on larger capital because of market scope and ability to employ more capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a small grocer may make 40–50% on a £100 stock, whereas a wholesale merchant may make only 8–10% on £10,000; the grocer must command sufficient recompense for the qualifications and tasks required despite limited capital employable in a narrow market.
